title: Feelings & opinions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: KOREAN DESCRIBING WORDS ARE VERBS. joayo ('is good'), masisseoyo ('is delicious'), bappayo ('is busy') each conjugate on their own and take NO copula in front of them. keopi-ga joayo is a whole sentence. Reaching for -ieyo here — keopi-ga joeun-ieyo — produces something that is not Korean at all, and it is the mistake an English speaker makes first.

joayo and joahaeyo are not the same word doing two jobs. joayo describes a thing: keopi-ga joayo, 'coffee is good'. joahaeyo says somebody likes something and takes an object: jeo-neun keopi-reul joahaeyo. The thing described takes -i/-ga; the thing liked takes -eul/-reul.

'Because' is an ending on the verb of the REASON, and the reason comes first: bappaseo jip-e gayo, 'being busy, I go home'. English can put its because-clause on either side; Korean puts the reason in front and the result behind, always.
The -aseo ending carries no tense. Whatever tense the sentence is in sits on the LAST verb, and the reason clause stays in its plain shape — which is one fewer thing to conjugate, not one more.
geuraeseo does the same job as -aseo but starts a new sentence: Pigonhaeyo. Geuraeseo jip-e isseoyo. Use the ending when you want one sentence and the connector when you want two.
wae ('why') stays in place like every other question word, and the answer normally comes back with -aseo on it. Question and answer end up the same shape, which makes the pair easy to practise.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1 — here as the thing being described, so it takes -ga.
'Is good' — one word, and a VERB: Korean's describing words conjugate like action verbs and take no copula. keopi-ga joayo is a complete sentence. Not M1's joahaeyo, 'like', which takes an object.

sentences.trap: There is no 'is' in this sentence and none is missing. joayo already contains it, because in Korean a describing word IS a verb — and adding the copula gives you a sentence with two verbs and no grammar.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-ga JO-ah-yo. The h inside the written word is silent, so it runs as jo-a-yo — the same silent h you met in joahaeyo, and the reason both words are spelled the way they are here.

variations.cue: The tea is good.
variations.changed: a different thing described

variations.cue: The coffee is delicious.
variations.changed: a different describing verb

variations.cue: The coffee is not good.
variations.changed: the negative — an in front, exactly as with any other verb

mistake.why: The copula has been added to a word that is already a verb. joayo is the whole predicate; nothing follows it.

sentences.usage: Saying what you think of something.
sentences.mnemonic: A describing word in Korean is already a verb.

words.note: 'This one', from M1.
'Is tasty'. Another describing verb, and you can hear isseoyo inside it — it was built long ago from 'taste' plus 'exists'. Learn it whole; the pieces are not taught separately here.

sentences.trap: You can hear isseoyo inside masisseoyo, and it is genuinely in there — but the word is learned whole. Trying to build it out of 'taste' plus 'exists' will give you something nobody says.
sentences.sound: EE-guh-nun ma-SI-ssuh-yo. The double ss in the middle is tense, pressed harder than an English s; it is the same tense sound as in isseoyo.

variations.cue: This is not delicious.
variations.changed: the negative

variations.cue: The tea is delicious.
variations.changed: a named thing rather than one you point at

variations.cue: This is good.
variations.changed: the other describing verb, and a milder judgement

mistake.why: The copula has been stuck onto a finished verb. masisseoyo is already the whole of 'is delicious'.

sentences.usage: Saying what something tastes like, at a table.
sentences.mnemonic: Verbs describe; nothing needs to be added.

words.note: 'I', from M1.
'Today', from M4.
'Is busy'. It describes a person, and like every describing word in Korean it is a verb — there is no 'am' in front of it. bappaseo is the same word wearing the 'because' ending.

sentences.trap: 'I am busy' has three words in English and two in Korean, because bappayo is doing the work of both 'am' and 'busy'. Looking for the 'am' is looking for a word the sentence has no room for.
sentences.sound: juh-nun O-neul BA-ppa-yo. The pp in the middle is tense — the lips press harder and no air escapes — and it is what separates bappayo from a soft b.

variations.cue: I am busy today.
variations.changed: the subject dropped

variations.cue: I am not busy today.
variations.changed: the negative

variations.cue: I am tired today.
variations.changed: another describing verb about a person

mistake.why: The copula again on a word that is already a verb. This is the same mistake three sentences running, and it is the one worth making three times.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you cannot do something.
sentences.mnemonic: Being busy is something you DO in Korean.

words.note: 'Why'. Like eodi and myeot it stays where it is and lets the voice ask the question — wae bappayo? — and the answer usually comes back with -aseo on it.
'Is busy'. It describes a person, and like every describing word in Korean it is a verb — there is no 'am' in front of it. bappaseo is the same word wearing the 'because' ending.

sentences.trap: wae sits at the front here because that is where it belongs in the sentence's own order, not because question words move. Put a subject in and wae stays exactly where it is, after it.
sentences.sound: WAE BA-ppa-yo, rising at the end. wae is one beat, close to English 'weh'.

variations.cue: Why are you tired?
variations.changed: a different state asked about

variations.cue: Why is Minsu busy?
variations.changed: a subject added — and wae does not move to the front

variations.cue: Why are you going to school?
variations.changed: an action rather than a state

mistake.why: wae has been put after the verb. Nothing follows the verb in a Korean sentence, question words included.

sentences.mnemonic: Question words stay put; the voice does the asking.

sentences.cue: I am busy because I am working.

words.note: 'Work', from M4, and here in its 'because' shape: ilhaeseo, 'because I work'. Every verb built on haeyo makes the shape the same way.
The 'because' ending. It goes on the verb STEM of the reason, and the reason comes FIRST: bappaseo jip-e gayo, 'being busy, I go home'. No tense of its own — that sits on the final verb.
'Is busy'. It describes a person, and like every describing word in Korean it is a verb — there is no 'am' in front of it. bappaseo is the same word wearing the 'because' ending.

sentences.trap: The reason comes FIRST. English can say 'I'm busy because I'm working' or 'because I'm working, I'm busy'; Korean has only the second order, and the ending is what marks the reason rather than a word at the front.
sentences.sound: il-HAE-suh BA-ppa-yo. The -seo at the end of ilhaeseo is unstressed and light — it is easy to swallow, and swallowing it removes the reason from the sentence.

variations.cue: I am going home because I am tired.
variations.changed: a different reason and a different result

variations.cue: I am not going because I am busy.
variations.changed: the result negated, and the reason clause untouched

variations.cue: I am tired because I work.
variations.changed: the same reason with a different result

mistake.why: The reason has been moved behind the result, English-style. The reason clause always comes first, and nothing at all follows the final verb.

sentences.mnemonic: Reason first, result second, verb last.

sentences.cue: I am going home because I am busy.

words.note: 'Is busy'. It describes a person, and like every describing word in Korean it is a verb — there is no 'am' in front of it. bappaseo is the same word wearing the 'because' ending.
The 'because' ending. It goes on the verb STEM of the reason, and the reason comes FIRST: bappaseo jip-e gayo, 'being busy, I go home'. No tense of its own — that sits on the final verb.
'Home', from M7 — where you go when you are busy, or stay when you are tired.
'Go', from M6.

sentences.trap: bappaseo has no tense in it. If the sentence were about yesterday, only the last verb would change — the reason clause would stay exactly as it is, which is one fewer thing to conjugate than English needs.
sentences.sound: BA-ppa-suh JI-be GA-yo. The tense pp is still there in the -aseo shape, and the ending is simply -seo after the stem's own a.

variations.cue: I am not going because I am busy.
variations.changed: the result negated

variations.cue: I am staying home because I am tired.
variations.changed: a different reason, and existence rather than going

variations.cue: I will go home because I am busy.
variations.changed: the future on the last verb only — the reason clause does not change

mistake.why: The past has been put into the reason clause. -aseo carries no tense: whatever tense the sentence has sits on the final verb.

sentences.usage: Giving a reason for what you are doing.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the last verb carries the tense.

sentences.cue: I am tired. So I am staying home.
sentences.glossEn: I am tired. That is why I am at home.

words.note: 'Is tired'. It ends in -haeyo, so it is built on the same 'do' verb as gongbuhaeyo — and its 'because' shape is pigonhaeseo, made the same way as every other.
'So, that is why' — the sentence-starting partner of -aseo: the same relationship, but opening a new sentence rather than joining a clause. Built from the same piece, hence the likeness.
'Home', from M7 — where you go when you are busy, or stay when you are tired.
'Is somewhere', from M7.

sentences.trap: geuraeseo starts a sentence; -aseo joins a clause. They say the same thing, and choosing between them is choosing whether you want one sentence or two — not a difference in meaning.
sentences.sound: pee-gon-HAE-yo. gu-RAE-suh JI-be i-SSUH-yo. There is a full stop in the middle and it should be heard: the first sentence falls, then geuraeseo starts the second.

variations.cue: I am staying home because I am tired.
variations.changed: the same thing said as one sentence with the ending

variations.cue: I am busy. So I am not going.
variations.changed: a different reason and a negated result

variations.cue: I am tired. So I will go home.
variations.changed: the future on the second sentence

mistake.why: The two sentences have been run together without a stop. geuraeseo begins a new sentence — if you want one sentence, the ending -aseo is what joins the clauses.

sentences.usage: Explaining yourself in two short sentences.
sentences.mnemonic: One connector for two sentences, one ending for one.

sentences.cue: The coffee is delicious. So I drink it every day.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1 — here as the thing being described, so it takes -ga.
'Is tasty'. Another describing verb, and you can hear isseoyo inside it — it was built long ago from 'taste' plus 'exists'. Learn it whole; the pieces are not taught separately here.
'So, that is why' — the sentence-starting partner of -aseo: the same relationship, but opening a new sentence rather than joining a clause. Built from the same piece, hence the likeness.
'Every day', from M4, still taking no marker.
'Drink', from M3.

sentences.trap: The second sentence has no object at all. English needs 'it'; Korean has just said what the coffee is, so repeating it — or supplying a pronoun — would be heavier than the sentence wants.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-ga ma-SI-ssuh-yo. gu-RAE-suh MAE-il ma-SHUH-yo. Two even sentences with a real pause between them.

variations.cue: The tea is delicious. So I drink it every day.
variations.changed: a different drink

variations.cue: The coffee is delicious. So I like it.
variations.changed: the liking verb from M1 in the second sentence

variations.display: Keopi-ga an masisseoyo. Geuraeseo an masyeoyo.
variations.script: 커피가 안 맛있어요. 그래서 안 마셔요.
variations.cue: The coffee is not good. So I do not drink it.
variations.changed: both halves negated

mistake.display: Keopi-ga masisseoyo. Geuraeseo i-geo-reul maeil masyeoyo.
mistake.script: 커피가 맛있어요. 그래서 이거를 매일 마셔요.
mistake.why: A word for 'it' has been supplied in the second sentence. The coffee was named a moment ago, so Korean drops it — putting it back makes the sentence point at something rather than continue smoothly.

sentences.usage: Giving an opinion and what follows from it.
sentences.mnemonic: Say it once; the second sentence remembers.

words.note: 'Why'. Like eodi and myeot it stays where it is and lets the voice ask the question — wae bappayo? — and the answer usually comes back with -aseo on it.
'Korean', the language, from M1.
'Learn', from M3.

sentences.trap: wae comes before the object here and after the subject when there is one. Its seat is at the front of what is being asked about, not at the front of the sentence — and it never drags anything with it.
sentences.sound: WAE han-GOONG-ma-rul BAE-wuh-yo, rising at the end. Two beats for wae and the object, then the verb.

variations.cue: Why will you study Korean?
variations.changed: the future, and wae does not move

variations.cue: Why does Minsu study Korean?
variations.changed: a subject in front, and wae sits behind it

variations.cue: Why are you going to Korea?
variations.changed: a different question with the same shape

mistake.why: A connector has been added at the end as if it were English's 'then'. geuraeseo begins a sentence and never ends one, and nothing follows the verb.

sentences.mnemonic: Ask in the shape the answer will take.

sentences.display: Hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geuraeseo hangungmal-eul baewoyo.
sentences.script: 한국에 갈 거예요. 그래서 한국말을 배워요.
sentences.cue: I will go to Korea. So I am studying Korean.
sentences.glossEn: I am going to go to Korea. That is why I am studying Korean.

words.note: 'Korea', from M1.
'Go', from M6.
The future's second half, from M6.
'So, that is why' — the sentence-starting partner of -aseo: the same relationship, but opening a new sentence rather than joining a clause. Built from the same piece, hence the likeness.
'Korean', the language, from M1.
'Learn', from M3.

sentences.trap: The reason here is in the future and the result in the present, and nothing has to be matched up between them. Each sentence carries its own tense, and geuraeseo simply joins the two.
sentences.sound: HAN-goo-ge gal GUH-ye-yo. gu-RAE-suh han-GOONG-ma-rul BAE-wuh-yo. Two full sentences, and the pause between them is where the connector gets its footing.

variations.display: Hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geuraeseo maeil gongbuhaeyo.
variations.script: 한국에 갈 거예요. 그래서 매일 공부해요.

mistake.why: The clause ending has been stuck onto a finished sentence. -aseo goes on a verb STEM; after a complete sentence you need geuraeseo and a full stop.

sentences.mnemonic: Two sentences, two tenses, one connector.
